 Written by Abhishek Jain Last Updated On: 19 Nov 2026 Published On: 19 Nov 2026 
 Table of Contents (click to expand) What Does A UV Camera Actually See?

 Can A UV Camera Tell You If Your Sunscreen Is Any Good? 
 So, Why Does Sunscreen Turn Your Face Black Under A UV Camera? 
 A UV camera records only ultraviolet light, and it paints anything that swallows ultraviolet as dark. Sunscreen's whole job is to swallow ultraviolet before it reaches your skin, so a face coated in it bounces almost none back to the camera and comes out black, even though nothing has changed in visible light. Mineral sunscreens go dark too, because zinc oxide and titanium dioxide absorb around 95 percent of the ultraviolet that hits them rather than reflecting it, a measurement that overturned the old idea that they work like tiny mirrors.
 A clip does the rounds every summer. Someone sits in front of a camera looking ordinary. They rub sunscreen into their face. Within seconds it turns the color of wet slate, as if the makeup department had got to them. Where the fingers missed, pale streaks remain, and the eyelids stay bright. It looks like a prank.
 Nothing visible has happened, of course. Switch back to a normal camera and the person is as pale as before. Whatever the second camera sees, your eyes cannot see it at all.
 So what is it seeing? And why does a cream that goes on white and dries clear look like paint to it? The answer ends with a claim about mineral sunscreen that fell apart when someone measured it.
 What Does A UV Camera Actually See?
 Sunlight is more than the light you can see. Past the violet end of the rainbow it carries ultraviolet. Those waves are shorter than visible light, and each packet carries more energy. Two bands reach the ground. UVB has the shortest waves and does the burning. UVA has longer waves and reaches deeper into skin. It even passes through window glass . Your eyes see none of it. The sensor in a digital camera does.
 That last part is the trick. The silicon chip in an ordinary camera responds to near-ultraviolet. Camera makers glue a filter over it at the factory to block UV and infrared. The first serious sunscreen camera was built at the University of Liverpool. The team took an ordinary DSLR and swapped that filter for a UV-only one. The sensor now records a world your eyes have never seen, and it prints it in grayscale.
 A surface that bounces ultraviolet back toward the lens comes out bright. A surface that swallows ultraviolet comes out dark. It asks one question of every point on your face: did the ultraviolet come back, or not?
 Where the sunscreen filters and the camera sit on the spectrum. Everything the article is about happens in the narrow ultraviolet strip to the left of the rainbow. 
 Bare skin already gives the camera plenty to say. Melanin, the pigment that darkens when you tan , exists to absorb ultraviolet, so it shows up dark. In the Liverpool photographs, faces that looked clear in daylight came out speckled. The team called the spots sun damage invisible to the naked eye. A study of 585 twelve-year-olds measured this hidden mottling. It was worst in children with freckles, red hair and light skin, the ones already known to be at higher risk from the sun.
 The same face with no sunscreen, photographed with a conventional camera and with the UV-sensitive camera. The spots on the right are pigment the eye cannot see. (Photo Credit: Lourenco et al. 2019, PLOS ONE, CC BY 4.0) 
 Why Does Sunscreen Make Your Skin Look Darker Under UV?
 Now put sunscreen on and look again. Most sunscreens rely on organic molecules, the so-called chemical filters, and avobenzone is one of the most common. Its job is to absorb ultraviolet before it reaches your skin cells.
 Light arrives in packets called photons. A photon's energy depends on its wavelength: shorter wave, bigger packet. Avobenzone has a chain of alternating double bonds between its two rings. A photon of the right size can kick the electrons in that chain up to a higher energy state. For avobenzone the sweet spot is a wavelength of 357 nanometers . It sits in the middle of the UVA band, right where the camera is looking. The molecule takes the hit, shuffles its shape, and sheds the energy mostly as a little heat. Then it is ready for the next photon.
 A UV photon needs nothing more to vanish. It does not bounce off the sunscreen and it does not reach your skin. To the camera, the face is now a surface that returns nothing, and nothing is black. The sunscreen has not changed color, and neither has your skin. The camera is showing you a map of where the ultraviolet died.
 The clip's eerie detail now makes sense too. The bright eyelids and hairline are the places the fingers never reached. Ultraviolet there bounces off bare skin and comes back as light.
 Avobenzone, the workhorse UVA filter. The chain of alternating bonds between the two rings is the part that catches the photon. (Photo Credit: Fvasconcellos, Wikimedia Commons, public domain) 
 Do Mineral Sunscreens Really Reflect UV Like Tiny Mirrors?
 If you use a mineral sunscreen, the kind with zinc oxide or titanium dioxide, you may have been told it works the other way. The story goes that mineral filters do not absorb UV but reflect it, like tiny mirrors. The US regulator wrote that into its first proposed sunscreen rule back in 1978. It said titanium dioxide scatters the rays rather than absorbing them. Labels have repeated it ever since. Even the American Academy of Dermatology still says so in its sunscreen FAQ.
 Which raises an obvious question. If mineral sunscreen reflected ultraviolet, a face coated in it should come out bright on the UV camera. It comes out black.
 In 2016 a team of sunscreen scientists measured the two effects . They spread zinc oxide and titanium dioxide in thin films on plastic plates. They put the plates in a hollow sphere that catches light going any way. Then they shone a lamp through the plates. The share of ultraviolet that came back out was 4 to 5 percent, less protection than SPF 2. Almost all of the rest, around 95 percent, was absorbed. The oxides did reflect plenty of light, but only at longer wavelengths. In visible light, 30 to 50 percent bounced back. So the cream looks white to your eyes and dark to the camera. In the authors' words, there is little remaining to be reflected.
 Why would a white powder behave like that? Because both oxides are semiconductors , like the silicon in the camera sensor. A semiconductor crystal has an energy gap. Before the crystal can absorb a photon, that photon has to kick an electron across the gap. A visible photon is too small a packet, so it passes through or bounces off. An ultraviolet photon clears the gap, and the crystal takes it. The switch is abrupt: zinc oxide absorbs hard below about 370 nanometers and lets light through above it. It is the same trick as avobenzone, done by a crystal instead of a molecule.
 One caveat: the 2016 test used raw oxides stirred into petroleum jelly, not a finished cream. The authors were clear that the finding changes nothing about how to use these sunscreens. It only changes the story on the label.
 How zinc oxide and titanium dioxide treat light, schematically. In the ultraviolet almost everything is absorbed and only a few percent bounces back; in visible light a third to a half bounces back, which is the white cast. Plateau values from the 2016 measurement; the curve shape is illustrative. 
 What Did UV Cameras Reveal About How People Apply Sunscreen?
 The Liverpool team did not build their camera for internet clips. They built it to answer a question nobody had checked. When people apply sunscreen the way they always do, which parts of the face do they miss?
 They photographed 57 volunteers before and after a routine coat of SPF 50, with no coaching. On average the volunteers missed about a tenth of the face. The eyelids came out twice as bad. A median 14 percent of the eyelid region was left bare, against 7 percent for the rest of the face. And 44 of the 57 people missed the inner corner of the eye. It is an unlucky place to skimp, because the skin around the eye is among the most cancer-prone on the body. The team's advice was to wear sunglasses that block UV.
 A follow-up with 84 volunteers compared a sunscreen with an SPF moisturizer of the same rating. With sunscreen, people missed about 11 percent of the face. With the moisturizer, about 17 percent. Before seeing their photographs, 77 of the 84 agreed they had covered their whole face. After seeing them, more than half changed their answer. Nobody had decided to skip their eyelids. They just had, with no way of knowing.
 It is also the quiet answer to a question people search every June. How do you know if your sunscreen is working? You cannot tell by looking. The label advice stands in for the camera. Apply it to dry skin about 15 minutes before you go out. Use about a shot glass of it for the exposed body. Reapply every two hours or so, and go back for the bits next to your eyes.
 Two volunteers before and after applying SPF 50 the way they normally would, photographed with the Liverpool UV camera. The bright patches are the places the fingers never reached. (Photo Credit: Pratt et al. 2017, PLOS ONE, CC BY 4.0) 
 Can A UV Camera Tell You If Your Sunscreen Is Any Good?
 Here the camera's talents run out, and it is worth being precise about where.
 The camera reports absorption in the band it happens to see. The Liverpool rig lit faces with UVA lamps, so it reported UVA coverage. The authors warned that they could not infer UVB protection from their pictures. SPF is a UVB number. It compares how much UV it takes to redden protected skin against bare skin. A face can go pleasingly black under a UVA camera and tell you nothing about SPF, or about how long the layer lasts.
 Nor does darker mean stronger in any useful way. SPF 30 blocks about 97 percent of UVB, and higher ratings add slivers on top. If you have wondered whether SPF 70 is overkill, it is mostly insurance. Dermatologists like the higher numbers for a reason the camera exposes. Most people put on a fraction of the amount used in the SPF test. A bigger number softens the penalty for a thin coat. A UV camera is a wonderful coverage check. It is a terrible strength meter.
 The share of UVB a sunscreen blocks, by its SPF. Doubling the number on the bottle barely moves the line. 
 So, Why Does Sunscreen Turn Your Face Black Under A UV Camera?
 Because the camera knows one thing about any point on your face: did ultraviolet come back from it? Sunscreen is engineered so that it does not.
 Three different absorbers show up in the clip, and the camera cannot tell them apart. Melanin, a pigment, darkens the freckles and the old sun damage you cannot see. Avobenzone and its cousins, organic molecules, swallow UVA photons in a chain of bonds. They let the energy go as warmth. The mineral crystals swallow any photon with enough energy to clear their gap. In practice that means almost all of the ultraviolet and almost none of the visible light. All three return nothing to the lens, and nothing is black.
 SPF 50 on the left half of the face only, photographed in visible light and in ultraviolet. Same face, same cream; only the camera changed. (Photo Credit: Spigget, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0) 
 The one thing the camera cannot do is lie about coverage. That is why it makes such an honest tool and such a popular clip. It will not tell you your SPF or how long the layer lasts. It will tell you, every time, that you missed your eyelids.
